4. It is also alleged that on 23-9-1986 this house was published in the abandoned property list through the gazette notification in the list of "Ka" and S1 No. 42. Despite the above, enlisting the house as an abandoned property on 20-4-1985 the Law Firm of the accused-petitioner Moudud Ahmed, namely, M/s Moudud Ahmed and Associates served a letter to the Bangladesh Bank on 9-8-1987 informing that Mr Moudud Ahmed has deposited the rent of the house upon a bank account and deposited money in “অনাবাসিক অবরুদ্ধ একাউন্ট” (Non-residential Blocked Account). The informant could not find any such account opened by Moudud Ahmed in the name of Manjur Ahmed or deposited any amount. Therefore, the FIR contains that the Ex. Minister, Mr Moudud Ahmed, by using the power of the government office and influenced during the period of 1978 to 2006 as Member of Parliament, Minister or government high official took steps for grabbing or misappropriating the aforementioned house in order to gain for himself illegally or for another. The market value of the property is around Taka 300 crores, as such, Moudud Ahmed and his brother Manjur Ahmed committed offences under section 5(2) of the Prevention or Corruption Act, 1947 and also under section 109 of the Penal Code. 

 8. The learned Advocate also submits that cognizance taken by a court is similar whether it is taken by a Special Court or by any other Criminal Court, in all circumstances the Judge has to consider the charge-sheet as to whether there is any prima facie case from the police report and after considering the police report Judge has to satisfy that there are sufficient elements present to take cognizance under section 190 of the Code of Criminal Procedure as well as section 4 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958. In support of his case the learned Advocate has drawn our particular attention to paragraph 43 and paragraph 48 of the case The State vs Joynal Abedin reported in 8 BLT 376 = 5 BLC 672 and, therefore, he prayed to make the Rule absolute. 

 12. Mr Md Khurshid Alam Khan, the learned Advocate appearing for the Opposite Party No. 2, the Durnity Daman Commission submits that the FIR was lodged against the present accused-petitioner and another alleging that the House of NW(H) 6, Holding No. 159, Gulshan Avenue, Gulshan- R/A, Dhaka appertains to a land measuring 1 bigha 13 khata and 14 chatak. The market value of the said property is Taka 300 crore and the same has been illegally grabbed or misappropriated by the accused-petitioner being a Minister, MP, High Officials of the Government during the year of 1973 until today and the charge-sheet No. 100 dated 17-12-2013 was filed in the court along with a sanction letter from the Durnity Daman Commission required under section 32 of the Durnity Daman Commission Act, 2004 as amended by the Act, 2013. 

 13. The learned Advocate also submits that after receiving the aforementioned required documents there were separate dates fixed by the learned Special Judge for taking cognizance but the present accused-petitioner submitted an application without any valid reason not to take cognizance. The petitioner sought adjournment from 22-6-2014 and until 14-9-2014 seeking time for hearing of the matter of cognizance and the learned Judge took cognizance by the impugned order under section 4 of the Act, 1958 sufficiently describing that the record of the case was before him and he heard regarding the matter of cognizance from the learned Advocates and finally taken cognizance of the offence, as such, there is no error of law in the impugned order, as such, the Rule issued in revisional application is liable to be discharged. 

 15. Considering the above submissions made by the learned Advocates for the respective parties and also considering the application under section 439 read with section 435 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and the annexures therein, in particular, the impugned order dated 14-9-2014, it appears to us that the First Information Report was submitted by Mr Harunur Rashid, the Deputy Director, Inquiry and Investigation of Durnity Daman Commission against the accused-petitioner and another on 17-12-2013 alleging that the accused petitioner has been using his official capacity as being the Minister, MP and other government official and has taken several steps to grave the house being House of NW(H) 6, Holding No. 159, Gulshan Avenue, Gulshan-R/A, Dhaka upon the land measuring 1 bigha 13 kata and 14 chatak by using certain documents despite the house was listed as an abandoned property published on a gazette notification on 23-9-1986 in its "Ka" list S1 No. 42. There is also allegation that the house was transferred on 10-8-1985 in the name of co-accused Manjur Ahmed, brother of the present accused-petitioner, despite the facts that the creator of the power of attorney in favour of one Mushin Darbar who died on 13- 3-1985.After investigation by the investigating officer of the case the charge-sheet was filed on 17-12-1913 containing almost aforementioned allegations and a sanction was issued from the Commission on 21-5-2014 and the same was filed in the court of learned Metropolitan Senior Special Judge, in Metropolitan Case No. 135 of 2014. 

 21. In this regard we refer two provisions of law in the criminal proceedings. Section 4 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958 has provided jurisdiction for the Special Judge and the cognizance to be taken by them. Similarly the sections 190 and 193 of the Code of Criminal Procedure are also provided for taking cognizance in the following manner:- 

 "4. Jurisdiction of Special Judges and cognizance of the cases by them.—(1) A Special Judge shall have jurisdiction within such territorial limits as may be fixed by the [Government] by notification in the Official Gazette and may take cognizance of any offence committed or deemed to have been committed within such limits and triable under this Act upon receiving a complaint of facts which constitute such offence or upon a report in writing of such facts made by any police officer." 

 [(2) The Government may, and subject to any general or special order issued in this behalf by the High Court Division, the Chief Judicial Magistrate may empower any Magistrate of the second or third class to take cognizance under sub-section (1) clause (a) or clause (b) of offences which he may try or send for trial.] 

 (3) The [Government] may empower any Magistrate of the second Class to take cognizance under sub-section (1), clause (c), of offences for which he may try or (send) for trial." 

 24. Another test as to taking cognizance in a case under either section 4 of the Act, 1958 or under sections 190 or 193 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is that the order passed by a court for taking cognizance with any languages, statements and decisions from which it can be inferred that he opted to apply his discretion to take cognizance. From the statements/words used in the present case it can be inferred from the above impugned order, in particular, the specific terms used by the learned Judge he opted to exercise his discretion to take cognizance. In this regard we hold that the laws regarding cognizance mentioned above the Judge, Magistrate or Court of Sessions has given discretion to take cognizance or not. We also hold that it can be inferred from the language used or word placed in the impugned dated 14-9-2014 order are sufficient as it is not the assumption or presumption but a logical inference can be drawn from the present impugned order and it is sufficient under the relevant provisions of law. The inference from the impugned order also includes that the court has considered the documents and records and after applying his judicial mind the learned court has taken cognizance as has been sufficient for taking cognizance as per the provisions of law thus no illegality has been committed by the learned Special Judge in passing the impugned order dated 14-9-2014. Accordingly, we are not inclined to interfere with the impugned order passed on 14-9-2014 for taking cognizance in his case.
